content: Participants reported that wheelchair services often fail to meet the comprehensive needs of users, with many parents expressing resignation to the current state of service provision. Specific issues highlighted include insufficient information about wheelchair options, their potential benefits, and available funding for families. Additionally, long waiting times, inadequate maintenance procedures, strict eligibility criteria, and differing opinions on user needs were common concerns. Despite these challenges, there was a general consensus that services were doing their best under the circumstances, leading to acceptance of the existing standards. Studies on tele-wheelchair assessments revealed mixed findings. While no significant differences were observed in consultation times between central and remote areas, tele-assessments reduced travel time for both healthcare professionals and wheelchair users. However, planning for tele-assessments took longer, though this was offset by the time saved on travel. Cost savings were also noted with tele-assessments. Feedback from wheelchair users indicated several benefits of tele-rehabilitation, such as reduced fatigue from travel, less stress from early appointments, decreased expenses, and improved direct communication with healthcare providers. However, some users expressed dissatisfaction with the quality of wheelchairs provided, citing issues such as poor design, lack of durability, and limited functionality. Training on wheelchair use and maintenance was identified as a critical area for improvement, with participants suggesting that both users and their families should receive comprehensive training. Satisfaction with wheelchair services varied widely. While some users reported being quite to very satisfied, others criticized the inconsistency and inefficiency of repair services, long waiting times, and the lack of critical replacement parts. Many users described the impact of inadequate services as a human rights issue, emphasizing the need for greater independence and mobility. The implementation of the World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines on wheelchair service provision showed some improvements in user satisfaction and mobility, particularly in less-resourced settings. However, gaps remained in follow-up services and training, especially for children. Comprehensive wheelchair services based on WHO guidelines were associated with improved mobility, independence, and participation in household activities, though challenges such as difficulty obtaining replacement parts and poor-quality wheelchairs persisted. Similarly, training programs based on WHO guidelines yielded inconsistent results regarding falls and other adverse events. Overall, while some progress has been made in improving wheelchair services, significant gaps remain in meeting the needs of users.
